summary: In multicast VPNs, customer multicast flows travel through tunnels in a provider network, advertised by BGP auto-discovery routes. This RFC adds wildcards so a single route can say that many customer flows share one tunnel.

plainLanguage.summary: In a multicast VPN, routers use routes to say which customer traffic uses each provider tunnel. RFC 6625 adds wildcard routes so one route can cover several flows instead of naming each flow separately.

subtitle: How MVPN routers use wildcard BGP routes to bind groups of customer multicast flows to tunnels.

tldr.problem: The MVPN routes defined before this RFC named one customer multicast flow at a time. They also lacked a route for making a selective tunnel the default for all flows.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 6625 allows a source, a group, or both to be represented by a wildcard in an S-PMSI A-D route. It defines how provider edge routers choose the matching route.
tldr.outcome: A provider edge router can originate fewer routes, improving control-plane scalability. The number of P-tunnels does not fall, so data-plane scalability is unchanged; later RFCs update this document.

today: RFC 6625 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 6514; it has been updated by RFC 7582, RFC 7900, and RFC 8534.

sections.title: Why Wildcard Routes Are Needed
sections.content:
A Multicast Virtual Private Network (MVPN) carries customer multicast traffic through tunnels in a service provider's network. The existing auto-discovery routes identify which tunnel carries a particular customer flow. Without wildcards, a separate route is needed for each flow bound to the same tunnel.

RFC 6625 extends Selective Provider Multicast Service Interface Auto-Discovery (S-PMSI A-D) routes with wildcard customer flow identifiers. The extension is optional. It can reduce the number of routes a provider edge (PE) router originates, but it does not reduce the number of tunnels.
sections.plainLanguage: A route can now describe a group of customer multicast flows instead of only one flow. This can reduce the number of routes routers need to announce.

sections.title: Customer Flows and Provider Tunnels
sections.content:
A customer multicast flow, or C-flow, is the ordered pair of a customer source address and a customer multicast group address, written (C-S,C-G). A provider tunnel (P-tunnel) carries traffic through one or more service providers' networks. An inclusive P-tunnel is joined by all PE routers attached to the MVPN; a selective P-tunnel is joined only by routers that need flows carried on it.

An S-PMSI A-D route is carried in a BGP Update. Its Network Layer Reachability Information (NLRI) identifies the customer flow pattern, while its PMSI Tunnel Attribute identifies the P-tunnel. RFC 6625 specifies procedures only for unidirectional, point-to-multipoint P-tunnels.
sections.plainLanguage: A flow identifies a source and a multicast group. A route connects that flow, or a group of flows, to a tunnel through the provider network.

sections.title: The Three Wildcard Patterns
sections.content:
The wildcard symbol is C-*. It can replace the source, the group, or both, producing (C-*,C-G), (C-S,C-*), and (C-*,C-*). The first pattern covers a specified group with any source; the second covers any group from a specified source; the third can represent a default route for all customer flows.

The RFC describes uses such as grouping flows on a shared tree or binding several flows from one source to a single tunnel. Some patterns apply only to particular multicast group types: (C-*,C-G) is specified for ASM groups, while (C-S,C-*) is specified for SSM groups.
sections.plainLanguage: A wildcard can mean any source, any group, or both. Each pattern applies only to the multicast cases described in the RFC.

sections.title: How a Wildcard Is Encoded
sections.content:
The S-PMSI A-D route's NLRI contains a source-length field and a group-length field. RFC 6625 defines a zero source length as a source wildcard and a zero group length as a group wildcard. When a length is zero, the corresponding address field is omitted.

A wildcard in a route applies only to multicast flows of the same address family as that route. The route format otherwise retains the existing MCAST-VPN NLRI structure, including the route distinguisher and originating router's IP address.
sections.plainLanguage: A zero length means that the matching source or group address is not specified. The wildcard only applies to addresses in the route's address family.

sections.title: Selecting a Matching Route
sections.content:
When a PE selects a route for a flow it transmits, it checks for an exact (C-S,C-G) route first. If none exists, it checks (C-S,C-*) for an SSM group, then (C-*,C-G) for an ASM group, and finally (C-*,C-*). A receiving PE applies the same preference among installed routes originated by its selected upstream PE.

Route choice does not depend on the order in which routes arrived. It can change when a route is advertised or withdrawn. A PE that originates a wildcard type must be able to process it, and must not originate it unless it is known that all PEs in that MVPN can process that type.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers check the most specific matching route first and use a broader wildcard only when needed. A router must know that the other routers can handle a wildcard before it advertises that type.

sections.title: Security and Status Today
sections.content:
RFC 6625 states that it adds no security considerations beyond those in the base MVPN specifications, RFC 6513 and RFC 6514. Its wildcard procedures extend the routes used to select tunnels.

RFC 6625 is a Proposed Standard and updates RFC 6514. Unit metadata lists later updates in RFC 7582, RFC 7900, and RFC 8534.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC points to the base MVPN documents for security considerations. It updates RFC 6514 and has later updates of its own.
